question: What size thresholds determine whether a UK company must participate in ESOS?
facts_present: 250 or more employees
OR annual turnover exceeding £44 million AND balance sheet total exceeding £38 million
OR condition — employee threshold is independent of financial thresholds
group structures assessed at highest UK-registered parent level

An organisation must participate in ESOS if it is a **large undertaking** on the **qualification date** (which is the 31 December immediately preceding each compliance deadline).

An organisation is a **large undertaking** for ESOS purposes if it meets **either** of the following criteria:

| Criterion | Threshold |
|-----------|-----------|
| Employees | 250 or more employees (full-time equivalent) |
| Turnover AND balance sheet | Annual turnover exceeding **£44 million** AND annual balance sheet total exceeding **£38 million** |

**Note:** The employee threshold is an OR condition with the financial thresholds — satisfying either employees ≥250, OR both financial thresholds, brings an organisation into scope.

For UK corporate groups, the qualification assessment applies at the **highest UK-registered parent level**. A UK subsidiary within a qualifying group is in scope regardless of its own size. Overseas parents are also assessed — a non-UK parent with UK-registered subsidiaries may qualify the UK entities for ESOS if the group as a whole meets the thresholds.

The Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme (ESOS) is a mandatory energy assessment scheme for large UK businesses, implemented under the **Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme Regulations 2014** (SI 2014/1643). It implements the UK's obligations under Article 8 of the EU Energy Efficiency Directive, retained and amended post-Brexit.

ESOS requires qualifying organisations to carry out comprehensive audits of their energy use across all buildings, industrial processes, and transport, and to identify cost-effective energy-saving opportunities. Participation does not require organisations to implement the identified measures — the obligation is to **audit and notify**, not to act.

---

Organisations that have a valid **ISO 50001** certification covering their total energy consumption are exempt from conducting separate ESOS audits (but must still notify compliance to the Environment Agency).

Public sector bodies are **not** required to participate in ESOS (they are subject to the Greening Government Commitments framework instead), although public sector-owned trading companies may be in scope.

---

The UK government has indicated that mandatory UK SDS will initially apply to:

- **UK premium and standard listed companies** (via FCA listing rule changes) — likely first wave
- **Large UK companies** meeting a size threshold (details under consultation) — likely second wave
- **Large private UK companies** — potentially in a later phase

The thresholds for unlisted companies have not been confirmed. The Companies Act 2006 definition of "large company" (two of three: >250 employees, >£36 million turnover, >£18 million balance sheet total) has been referenced as a likely basis, but the government has indicated a higher threshold may apply initially.

The Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (EU Directive 2022/2464) entered into force on 5 January 2023. It replaces the Non-Financial Reporting Directive (NFRD) and significantly expands the scope, detail, and assurance requirements for sustainability reporting across the EU.

The CSRD requires in-scope companies to report on environmental, social, and governance (ESG) matters using the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRS), developed by the European Financial Reporting Advisory Group (EFRAG). Reporting must appear in a dedicated section of companies' management reports and must be independently assured.

Although the UK is no longer an EU member state, the CSRD is directly relevant to many UK-headquartered businesses. This document sets out when and how.

CSRD reports require **limited assurance** by an accredited independent auditor or assurance service provider from Wave 1. The European Commission may move to **reasonable assurance** in subsequent phases.

UK companies providing data to EU subsidiaries for group-level CSRD reports should note that the data they supply will ultimately be subject to this assurance requirement.

A UK-based parent company falls into CSRD scope under Article 40 (the "third-country undertaking" provision) if:

- It generated **net turnover exceeding €150 million** in the EU in each of the last two consecutive financial years, **AND**
- It has at least one of the following EU-based entities:
  - A **large EU subsidiary** (meeting the large company thresholds — see Section 3)
  - An EU-regulated-market-**listed subsidiary** (regardless of size)
  - An EU **branch** generating net turnover exceeding €40 million in the previous financial year

The Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme (ESOS) is a mandatory energy assessment scheme for large UK businesses, implemented under the **Energy Savings Opportunity Scheme Regulations 2014** (SI 2014/1643). It implements the UK's obligations under Article 8 of the EU Energy Efficiency Directive, retained and amended post-Brexit.

ESOS requires qualifying organisations to carry out comprehensive audits of their energy use across all buildings, industrial processes, and transport, and to identify cost-effective energy-saving opportunities. Participation does not require organisations to implement the identified measures — the obligation is to **audit and notify**, not to act.

---

Organisations that have a valid **ISO 50001** certification covering their total energy consumption are exempt from conducting separate ESOS audits (but must still notify compliance to the Environment Agency).

Public sector bodies are **not** required to participate in ESOS (they are subject to the Greening Government Commitments framework instead), although public sector-owned trading companies may be in scope.
